newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Highlights of APEC members' action plans.
newsitem.headline: Highlights of APEC members' action plans.

text.p: After a year's worth of meetings, revisions and consultations, APEC's 18 member economies have finalised detailed plans for setting up the world's biggest free trade area.

These are contained in Individual Action Plans outlining how each economy plans to gradually move towards the grouping's goal of lowering all trade barriers by 2010 for its developed economies such as the United States and Japan and 2020 for its less well-off members such as Papua New Guinea.
Following are highlights of the action plans, which leaders of Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum members are expected to endorse at their summit on Monday.

AUSTRALIA - Generally goes beyond World Trade Organisation (WTO) commitments. Plans to reduce tariffs, currently averaging 6.1 percent compared with 18.2 percent in 1988, to between zero and five percent by 2000. To introduce business travel card this year to make access easier for foreign executives.
BRUNEI - Plans to fix 82 percent of total tariff lines at 5.0 percent, going beyond its WTO commitments.

CANADA - Strongly supports Information Technology Agreement to remove tariffs on these products by 2000 and is prepared to discuss similar arrangements on oilseeds, non-ferrous metals, wood products, fish products and electronics.
CHILE - Exceeds WTO commitments on tariff reductions and aims to complete most trade and investment liberalisation by 2010 rather than APEC's 2020 deadline for developing economies.
CHINA - Plans to reduce average tariff to 15 percent by 2000 from the current 23 percent. Aims also to boost foreign participation in banking, insurance, transport, telecommunications and retailing.
HONG KONG - All Hong Kong's APEC commitments go beyond WTO and it aims for zero tariffs by 2010. Also plans to study introducing business travel pass scheme by 1997-98.
INDONESIA - Plans to lower all tariffs to a zero to 10 percent range by 2003. Also plans to privatise state enterprises covering the steel industry, services, shipping and railways.

JAPAN - Plans to align product standards with the rest of the world and to speed up its quarantine control procedures for animal and plant product imports. Says it will introduce a "wide range of deregulatory measures for structural reform, with a view to realising an economic society which is open to the world".
SOUTH KOREA - Pledges to remove all non-tariff barriers on all items, except rice, by 2001 and to open up more sectors to foreign involvement.
MALAYSIA - Foreign equity of up to 49 percent to be permitted in domestic brokerages.

MEXICO - Willing to speed up tariff reductions if other APEC members agree to do so. To eliminate the 49 percent limit on foreign direct investment in the automotive industry by 1999 and by 2004 will permit 100 percent foreign ownership of international land transport.
NEW ZEALAND - Already exceeds WTO commitments and pledges further liberalisations.
PAPUA NEW GUINEA - Aims to simplify cumbersome procedures for approving foreign investments.
PHILIPPINES - Aims to reduce tariffs to a uniform 5.0 percent by 2004 except for sensitive agricultural items. To remove some remaining barriers to foreign ownership in financial sector.
SINGAPORE - To remove all tariffs by 2010. To speed up liberalisation of basic telecommunications sector and to meet other commitments ahead of schedule.
TAIWAN - To reduce tariffs to an average 6.0 percent by 2010. Also plans to remove bans on some agricultural imports when it accedes to WTO.

THAILAND - Goes beyond its WTO commitments in most sectors and in the rest fully complies with its earlier APEC commitments. To allow privately owned ports, higher foreign participation in the insurance industry and to liberalise natural gas and power generation.
UNITED STATES - Says it is determined to set the pace in any areas where it has not already met or exceeded its APEC and WTO commitments.
